title: Order checkout failing
executive_summary: INC-007 (SEV2): order checkout error rate rose above 25% starting around 15:23Z on 2026-09-20, against a symptom start of 15:25Z and report at 15:31Z. Final status is ROOT_CAUSE_IDENTIFIED with confidence 0.6. The most probable explanation is configuration regression cfg-7f81d14a (OPS-2375, applied as config reload v42 at 15:22:00Z), which cut order-service payment_client.timeout_ms from 3000 to 300. Calls from order-service to payment-service POST /v1/charges that exceed 300ms now fail client-side. Those failures opened the payment circuit breaker (15:24:10Z) and exhausted the payment retry budget (15:25:13Z), producing checkout failures. Order-service error rate moved from a baseline of about 0.6% to a window mean of 11.7% (max 32%), and timeout rate from 0.1% to 13.2% (max 35.7%) (met-order-service-error_rate-1510-1531, met-order-service-timeout_rate-1510-1531). Payment-service latency and error metrics stayed flat, so the failures sit on the order side (met-payment-service-p50/p95_latency_ms-1510-1540). Payment team's health assessment is consistent with this finding. Alternative hypotheses were rejected: order-side resource saturation (H4) and payment 5.8.1 deployment regression (H2).

hypotheses.description: Config change cfg-7f81d14a (OPS-2375, applied as config reload v42) cut order-service payment_client.timeout_ms from 3000 to 300 at 15:22Z. Calls from order-service to payment-service POST /v1/charges that exceed 300ms now fail client-side, which opens the payment circuit breaker and exhausts the payment retry budget. Mechanism: timeout_ms 3000->300 (15:22:00Z, reload v42) -> order-service PaymentClient times out on slow charge calls (first timeout 15:23:20Z) -> error_rate ~0.6%->~30% and timeout_rate ~0.1%->~35% (15:23) -> breaker OPEN 15:24:10Z and retry budget exhausted 15:25:13Z -> checkout failures. Payment server-side metrics stay healthy because the failing calls are judged against the new client cap, not against a server error.

critic_review.summary: Leading hypothesis H1: the order-service payment_client.timeout_ms change (3000 -> 300, cfg-7f81d14a, reload v42 at 15:22:00Z) caused client-side timeouts on POST /v1/charges, which opened the payment circuit breaker and drove checkout failures. Support: the only order-service config change in the window, timing matches (reload 15:22:00, first timeout 15:23:20, error/timeout onset 15:23, breaker open 15:24:10), and the error text literally reports a 300ms timeout. Payment server-side metrics are flat (p50/p95/p99, error and timeout rates), so the failures are on the order side. Order-service CPU, memory, DB connection utilisation and request rate are all flat across 15:10-15:40 (checked this round), which removes resource saturation as a driver. H4 (order-side pool wait/queueing) has no supporting resource or pool evidence and its only signal, the p95 tail rise, is itself consistent with the timeouts; rejected in favour of H1. H2 (payment 5.8.1 deploy) is contradicted by flat payment latency, error and timeout metrics at 14:40 and 15:23; rejected.

assessments.reasoning: Config change is the only order-service change in window, precedes the first timeout by ~80s, matches the timeout error text and breaker timing, and order-side resources are flat. Payment-side server metrics are healthy, consistent with client-side cap. Limitation: a 300ms cap alone would imply only ~1% of calls exceed it given payment p99 ~300ms, which is lower than the observed ~35% timeout share, so the exact latency distribution on the order side is not fully explained. This does not change the culprit or category.

No pool-wait, network, or queue evidence was collected. Order CPU, memory, db_conn_util and request rate are flat, and the order p95 rise is a downstream symptom of the timeout behaviour. A separate order-side cause is not supported, and the 10x timeout change is a sufficient explanation.

Only temporal correlation with the 14:40 deploy. Payment p99, p50, error rate and timeout rate are flat at both 14:40 and 15:23, so there is no evidence of slower charge calls. The 43-minute delayed onset is unexplained.

Notify the payment team that payment-service metrics were healthy throughout, so their service should not be changed as part of this mitigation.
preventive_actions: Add validation to config changes so that payment_client.timeout_ms values are checked against the observed p95/p99 latency of POST /v1/charges before rollout, and require review for changes of more than an order of magnitude (OPS-2375 process).
Stage config reloads with canary instances and automated rollback on error-rate or timeout-rate regression.
Review the order-service circuit breaker and retry budget settings so that client-side timeout misconfiguration cannot exhaust the retry budget this quickly.
monitoring_recommendations: Alert on order-service timeout_rate above 1% for 2 minutes, and on payment circuit breaker OPEN events (logpat-order-service-e2b30f44).
Log and alert on config reload events and emit the effective payment_client.timeout_ms value per instance, so read-back confirms the active setting.
Track order-service to payment-service call latency histogram (client-side) alongside payment-service server-side latency to separate client and server causes.
Monitor order-service connection-pool wait time and order-to-payment network latency, which were not directly queried in this investigation and remain the main unverified alternative (H4).
limitations: Confidence values are rule-based evidence-strength scores, not calibrated probabilities.
Investigation terminated because: critic verdict APPROVED
conclusion: The most probable root cause of INC-007 is the order-service payment_client.timeout_ms reduction from 3000 to 300ms in config reload v42 (cfg-7f81d14a, 15:22:00Z). It produced client-side timeouts on POST /v1/charges, which opened the payment circuit breaker and exhausted the retry budget. This is a probable explanation rather than a fully confirmed one: the confidence is 0.6, the running timeout value on every instance has not been read back, and the magnitude of the timeout share has not been fully reconciled with the payment latency distribution. Reverting the config is the immediate mitigation. Closing the read-back and pool/network evidence gaps should follow.
